prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological invariant of time-reversal-invariant band insulators, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B039 as a single-part prize and my preferred configuration has not changed since round 1. What I have refined is the scope. The Kane-Mele Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall proposal, followed by Molenkamp's observation of helical edge transport in HgTe wells, is a complete chain from a new principle to a measurement that could have failed. The principle is that band topology, protected by time-reversal symmetry and driven by spin-orbit coupling, classifies electronic phases without any broken symmetry. It has been confirmed for almost two decades by transport, photoemission and scanning probes in several material families, and it is the area where first-principles band-structure calculations and experiment have worked together most directly. In answer to the chair, what is new relative to 2016 can be said in one sentence: the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and integer quantum Hall-type phases, which need a magnetic field or a particular model, whereas this achievement is a topological classification of real, time-reversal-invariant materials with a symmetry-protected invariant and a measured edge conductance. I treat the round-1 count of five supporters as secondary to this argument. The three names are each decisive for a distinct step (the invariant, the proposal, the experiment) and fit within the three-laureate cap without any stretching.
statement.case_against: The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang remains the real weakness, because their HgTe proposal told Molenkamp where to look, and Zhang's death in 2018 means it cannot be repaired by adding a name. The 3D topological-insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others also lies outside the credit, so a citation worded around topological insulators in general would overclaim. I regard a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant as the honest wording, but it does not remove the criticism that a theory that enabled the experiment is not credited by name. The overlap with 2016 will also be contested by some members, and applications are still limited, so the case is conceptual and experimental rather than technological. Compared with B022, this prize has the harder allocation and B022 the cleaner one, and I do not claim that a cleaner allocation counts for nothing.

responses.point: Kroll keeps the optical lattice clock (B022) first on the basis of a clean two-name credit, a concrete and measurable impact, and a citation that can separate the neutral-atom magic-wavelength idea from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, while conceding that topological insulators have wider influence across condensed matter.
responses.response: I accept the clean credit as B022's main advantage, and his concession on breadth is fair. My disagreement is about how to weigh the two attribution problems that the chair asked us to compare. For B039 the people left out have genuine claims, but the three named are individually decisive for the step they are credited with. For B022 the credit is clean only if one accepts that Katori and Ye define the achievement, while Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat and the ion-clock groups are excluded and Ye's role is partly about precision and many-body control that the community shares. The lattice clock also remains a third recognition in the metrology lineage, which Kroll himself lists as his strongest reservation. If the committee judges the BHZ omission to be disqualifying, B022 is my first alternative, but I do not think the omission is a better reason to defer than the metrology overlap is for the clock.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is not a repeat of 2005 or 2012 because it interrogates many neutral atoms at once, and she cautions that strong opening support for B039 should not be mistaken for a weaker scientific case for B022.
responses.response: I agree that opening counts are not scientific evidence and I have tried not to rest on them. I find the many-atoms argument persuasive as a scientific distinction, since it changes the statistics and the systematics in a way that a single-ion clock cannot. Where I differ is on how distinct it is as a prize achievement, since the same laser-spectroscopy lineage and the same clock-comparison infrastructure underlie all three. I would ask her whether the redefinition of the second, once it happens, would settle her own timing doubt. If it does, B022 becomes a stronger candidate next year, and I do not think that defers it unfairly. I also note that she herself lists the question of a B039 prize built with the BHZ credit, and my answer is that the supplied names cannot do that, so scoping the citation is the only option within the rules.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved B039 to the front after reading the opening ballots, stated that this is a change caused by colleagues' evidence, and proposed a citation scoped to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant so that it matches the three names without implying that the whole field is credited.
responses.response: I support that scoping and I have adopted similar wording above. I would add one point to his experimentalist argument: the HgTe result is persuasive because the quantised edge conductance in a small, ballistic device was a prediction that could have failed, and the Molenkamp group had to grow the quantum wells at the quality needed. His acknowledgement that he cannot verify the priority history from the files is the honest position, and I share it. I would not go as far as writing the omitted theorists into the citation, since that would imply a credit the three-laureate cap does not allow. I would prefer the committee's explanatory text, not the citation, to note that the BHZ proposal and the 3D work are outside this prize and are recognised there as such.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes a two-part prize of B022 and B003, a precision-measurement achievement plus the IceCube discovery, and admits that B003 is the weakest part because a collaboration-scale discovery has a single name credited.
responses.response: I respect his willingness to name the weakness of his own configuration, and the chair's summary says he would rather see B022 or B039 stand alone than keep a thin B003 credit. On that basis there may be less distance between us than the first-round ranking suggests. I still do not support B003 here, because one name for a detector collaboration, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal outside the credit and the flux sources unidentified, is a weaker allocation than any other on the shortlist. A two-part prize built to span subfields is also a goal I would not set against the quality of the individual parts. If he is asked to choose between B022 alone and B039 alone, I would ask him which allocation he finds easier to defend, and I expect that answer to decide whether we agree.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers is disqualifying for other members; I rely on recollection for the priority history, as do several colleagues, and none of us can verify it from the supplied files.

Whether a citation scoped to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant is enough to avoid looking dismissive of the omitted theorists, or whether the committee will want the 3D work covered, which no available three-name credit allows.
How much of the 2016 distinction (time-reversal-invariant materials against quantum Hall and Haldane-type phases) is accepted by members who list the overlap as a reservation.
Whether a formal redefinition of the SI second would change the ranking between B022 and B039, and whether the pending status counts as a maturity criterion at all.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. None of the credited names for B039, B022 or B035 appears among my documented connections (my doctoral supervisor, Los Alamos colleagues, co-authors of my books and Uppsala Materials Theory colleagues), so I see no ground for recusal. My field, first-principles electronic structure and magnetism, is adjacent to topological band theory and I flag that as a possible bias towards condensed-matter candidates, which is why I have tried to rest my case on the allocation and the 2016 distinction and not on field affinity. I note the chair's flags for Johansson and Kroll and none of them affects B039.
